newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Bulgarians still suffer from communist legacy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bulgarians still suffer from communist legacy.

text.p: Bulgaria's efforts to restore property seized under communist rule are creating a legal dilemma as families are forced out of homes they have lived in for decades.
The Civil Movement of Victims of the Restitution says about 100,000 households face eviction.
Some Bulgarians, like 86-year-old Stanimir Temchev, are double victims, having experienced both communist repression and the hardship caused by moves to reverse it.
His original home was seized when the communists took power, and his present apartment is among those to be returned to its original owners under the restitution law.
Temchev was a prosperous local activist of the anti-communist Bulgarian Agrarian National Union in the western Kyustendil region when the communists took power in September 1944.
He and his family were interned in 1950 and forced to settle in the northeastern village of Tataritsa. His land and house were seized by the state.
His internment ended in 1956, the year Todor Zhivkov took power to rule the Balkan country until 1989.
"We settled in the coal miners' town of Pernik but for two years my father was refused any job as he was seen as an enemy of the people," recalled his daughter Lilyana Stanimirova.

She said she was not allowed to apply for a university place because of her father. To win a place she first had to become a leading activist of the Sofia branch of the Communist Youth League, the Komsomol.
More than three decades later, Stanimirova is a chemical engineer living with her father, her two sons and their families in a flat rented by the municipality in Sofia.
"One injustice cannot be mended by replacing it with another injustice," Stanimirova said.

"I have experienced the communist repressions myself and I am not against restitution," she said. "But the state has washed its hands of the matter and has left us to sue each other in court in a very humiliating way."
Under a 1948 property law, all apartments, houses, and shops deemed surplus to their owners' needs were seized by the communist state.
Stanimirova said she understood the owners had a right to their property but Bulgaria's economic crisis meant it was impossible for her family to buy another apartment.
Under the restitution law passed in February 1992, Bulgaria must return property seized by the former communist government from 1947 to 1952 to its pre-communist owners or their heirs.
BAD HOUSING AND SHORTAGES CREATE ADDITIONAL PROBLEMS
The law envisaged a three-year moratorium on reclaiming property rented from the state to help tenants find alternative accommodation.
But that is no easy task in a country where more than 30 towns suffer housing shortages, and five percent of the housing stock is deemed uninhabitable and 30 percent substandard.
City authorities are trying to resolve the problem, but say a lasting solution is possible only when the housing stock increases.
The three-year limit expired in February 1995, leaving many owners and tenants at the mercy of the courts.
Pavlina Penkova, a historian at the Chief Archives Directorate, said both owners and tenants were affected.

"Owners are unable to recover their property seized by the communists while tenants in turn face eviction and are to become homeless without having any guilt for the repression by the previous authorities."

Last month some 30 people staged a week-long protest in front of parliament to draw attention to their plight. They attracted little response and now plan to appeal to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.
"The deeds of the former authorities have caused a lot of suffering in the past, but now the consequences of their deeds are no less painful," Penkova said.
"They could not imagine that sometime they would be toppled -- they treated the seized property as if their regime would last forever."
